body:
Each scalar window asks the quantum computer to add one known table point to its current accumulator. The window construction determines which point to use. Here we follow the addition itself and see how two coordinate registers can hold the calculation from beginning to end.

Turn two coordinates into the next point

The address \(j\) selects the table point coherently, so different branches can add different points without measuring the address. Coordinates are 256-bit elements of \(\mathbb F_p\), with \(p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977\). We first follow the generic addition, where the operands of division and in-place multiplication are nonzero; the exceptional inputs are identified below.

Write the accumulator as \(A=(x_1,y_1)\) and the selected point as \(T_j=(x_2,y_2)\). Subtracting coordinates gives \(\Delta x=x_1-x_2\) and \(\Delta y=y_1-y_2\), whose ratio is the slope \(\lambda\). The new coordinates satisfy \[x_3=\lambda^2-x_1-x_2,\qquad y_3=\lambda(x_2-x_3)-y_2.\] We want to obtain these coordinates while preserving \(j\), implementing \(|j,A\rangle\mapsto|j,A+T_j\rangle\). The order of updates is chosen to reuse the two live registers.

Why a gcd circuit appears inside point addition

Division in the field means multiplication by an inverse. For example, \(3\cdot5-2\cdot7=1\) shows that 3 is the inverse of 5 modulo 7. Extended Euclid produces the same kind of identity for \(\Delta x\) and \(p\), giving the multiplier needed to turn \(\Delta y\) into the slope.

The circuit saves space by recording the binary-gcd reductions and applying those reductions directly to \(\Delta y\). It obtains the quotient without retaining a separate inverse. The gcd lesson first works through a small division, then explains the cheaper signed reductions used here.

The division circuit shows the complete sequence: construct the record, apply it to the numerator, and erase the record. That cleanup is what makes its workspace available to the next stage of point addition.

Follow the two live registers

After division, the second register holds \(\lambda\). Add \(3x_2\) to the first and subtract \(\lambda^2\); it now holds \(x_2-x_3\). Multiplying the second register by this value turns the slope into \(y_3+y_2\). The final offsets then recover \(x_3,y_3\), as the trace below shows.

OperationFirst registerSecond register
Subtract table coordinates\(\Delta x\)\(\Delta y\)
Divide\(\Delta x\)\(\lambda\)
Add \(3x_2\); subtract square\(x_2-x_3\)\(\lambda\)
Multiply\(x_2-x_3\)\(y_3+y_2\)
Remove offsets; negate x\(x_3\)\(y_3\)

Release workspace; keep track of its phase

Keeping the loaded table coordinates throughout this calculation would occupy another \(2n\) qubits. Instead, the circuit clears them after use by X measurement. If \(m\) is the string of measurement results and \(f(j)\) the loaded bits, the retained address acquires a known sign: \[\sum_j\alpha_j|j,f(j)\rangle\longrightarrow\sum_j\alpha_j(-1)^{m\cdot f(j)}|j\rangle.\] Here \(m\cdot f(j)\) is their binary inner product. The first and third lookups load the same coordinates, so their correction masks combine by XOR; the \(3x_2\) lookup has its own mask.

Measurement frees the qubits; feedforward preserves coherence

This is measurement-based uncomputation. Measure the loaded bits, keep their outcomes classically, and reset those qubits for new work. It releases up to 512 coordinate qubits before division. The address remains coherent because its induced phase is known and later repaired.

The required repair depends on what was erased. Erasing a copied bit needs a Z correction; erasing an AND needs CZ. Erasing the coordinate function \(F(j)\) requires the phase \((-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}\), generally implemented by another lookup. The lookup lesson derives that correction and shows its circuit.

Two randomizations, two purposes

The circuit uses randomness for two distinct reasons. A group offset avoids identity table entries; a field mask controls the distribution entering approximate arithmetic.

Move the table away from infinity

The tables also simplify exceptional-case handling. For window \(i\), store \([j2^{iw}+\mu_i]P\), choosing the classical offset \(\mu_i\) so no entry is the point at infinity. Every branch receives the same fixed group shift, so equality between oracle outputs—and therefore the Fourier relation—is preserved.

Make the square target uniform

A separate field mask makes the square-subtraction target uniform for the failure analysis. Add a random \(R\), subtract \(\lambda^2\), then remove \(R\); the net update is unchanged. Loading \(3x_2+R\) directly from the table can combine the first mask addition with the lookup.

Where this saving stops

For the selected point \(T\), the generic construction excludes \(A\in\{\mathcal O,T,-T,-[2]T\}\). The last case makes \(x_2-x_3=0\), so multiplication cannot reversibly remove the slope. Appendix B counts these exceptions together with failures of the approximate arithmetic and phase repair.

Under the arithmetic comparison's executed-gate convention, one addition uses about \(1.196\times10^6\) Toffoli-type operations before three lookups. Thus \(28(1.196\times10^6+3\cdot2^{16})\approx39.0\times10^6\), using the largest observed count in 100 runs. The full compiled schedule uses its own accounting and contains 40,420,330 injections, with a peak of 1457 logical qubits.

title: V. High-level implementation of point addition

body:
Why point addition needs a gcd computation

Suppose we need to divide 4 by 5 modulo 7. We are looking for a number that gives remainder 4 when multiplied by 5. The answer is 5, because 25 leaves remainder 4. Point addition needs this same operation on 256-bit numbers: the numerator and denominator are differences between two points' coordinates.

The two points are the accumulator \((x_1,y_1)\) and a selected table point \((x_2,y_2)\). Subtract their coordinates to obtain \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\). Their ratio is the slope used to compute the sum. For a nonzero denominator in the prime field, we can write that ratio as multiplication by an inverse:

\[\lambda=\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}=\Delta y\,(\Delta x)^{-1}\pmod p.\]

We can find the inverse by reducing the denominator together with the prime. Euclid's algorithm expresses their greatest common divisor as an integer combination of the two inputs. Here that divisor is 1. Reducing the resulting identity modulo the prime removes the prime's contribution and leaves the inverse:

\[a\Delta x+bp=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a\Delta x=1\pmod p\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=(\Delta x)^{-1}\pmod p.\]

In our example, Euclid gives \(3\cdot5-2\cdot7=1\). Thus multiplying by 3 undoes multiplication by 5 modulo 7. Applying it to the numerator gives \(4\cdot3=12\equiv5\). We have now obtained the quotient through a computation on the denominator and the prime.

A quantum circuit could store that inverse and then multiply by it. The paper saves space by keeping the sequence of reductions instead. Binary gcd uses only swaps, subtractions, and halving. Once those decisions have been recorded, the same sequence can act directly on the numerator.

The Dialog construction makes this precise. It records the denominator's reduction, replays the record on a pair containing the numerator and zero, and reverses record construction. The complete operation preserves the denominator, replaces the numerator by the quotient, and returns the working qubits to zero:

\[|\Delta x\rangle|\Delta y\rangle|0\rangle_{\rm work}\longmapsto|\Delta x\rangle|\Delta y(\Delta x)^{-1}\bmod p\rangle|0\rangle_{\rm work}.\]

For the 256-bit problem, this avoids retaining a separate 256-bit inverse. The record itself occupies space, but the circuit stores it where the shrinking gcd remainders have released qubits. We can now ask how to make each recorded reduction cheaper.

The circuit below shows the three stages: build the record, apply it, and erase it. The full replay lesson follows an example through all three. In this lesson we focus on the arithmetic inside the first stage.

Change what is stored, then simplify the gate

Consider one reduction of integer remainders \(u,v\), with \(u\) odd. If \(v\) is even, we can halve it immediately. If \(v\) is odd, we first subtract the suitably oriented odd remainder, making the difference even. A stored bit records which branch occurred, so the quantum computation can later reverse the step.

Let \(a\) be the low bit of \(v\): it is 0 for the even branch and 1 for the odd branch. Once any required swap has put the operands in the right order, both cases are expressed by \[v'=\frac{v-au}{2}.\] The expensive operation therefore has a control choosing subtraction or no subtraction. IonQ changes the stored value so this choice becomes addition or subtraction, which uses a cheaper carry circuit.

An odd register exposes the next parity

For example, take \(u=3,v=8\). Instead of storing the even value 8, store \(8+3=11\). For an odd value such as \(v=5\), store 5 unchanged. Both stored values are now odd. In general this is \(\widetilde v=v+(1-a)u\). Subtracting \(u\) from it gives twice the ordinary next remainder, so the next parity follows from just the second-lowest bits: \[a'=v'\bmod2=\widetilde v[1]\oplus u[1].\] Both lowest bits are 1, so no borrow enters that comparison. Re-expressing the next remainder in the same odd convention gives \[\boxed{\widetilde v'=\frac{\widetilde v+(-1)^{a'}u}{2}.}\] The two rows below show the addition and subtraction branches separately.

Ordinary inputStored inputParity from bit 1Stored update
\((3,8)\)\((3,11)\)\(1\oplus1=0\)\((11+3)/2=7\)
\((3,5)\)\((3,5)\)\(1\oplus0=1\)\((5-3)/2=1\)

After the signed update, we must orient the remainders for the following step. The swap bit is \(m=a'[u>\widetilde v']\), where the bracket is 1 when its condition holds. Thus only the odd branch requires a comparison. Keeping this decision in the record lets the inverse circuit undo the swap.

One adder supplies both signs

To see why signed addition helps, complement every bit of a width-\(w\) target. This changes \(z\) to \(J(z)=2^w-1-z\). Add \(u\), then complement again: \[J(J(z)+u)=z-u\pmod{2^w}.\] A control bit can turn both complements on or off using CNOTs. The carry circuit always performs the same addition; it does not need an extra control at each carry.

The replay must use a matching change of variables. For field registers \(r,s\), the paper stores \(\widetilde s=s-(1-a)r\), giving the partner update \(\widetilde s'=\widetilde s-(-1)^{a'}r\pmod p\). Here \(r\) denotes a register, not the curve's group order. Recorded swaps and the required modular halves or doubles complete the replay.

The prime-modulus boundary still matters

The integer complement identity needs attention when used in a prime field. For \(p=2^n-c\), complementing gives \(J(z)\equiv-z+c-1\pmod p\). The constant cancels around an exact modular adder, but \(c-1\) inputs produce bit strings at least \(p\). The circuit must account for those representations, including its approximate \(0\leftrightarrow p\) correction when a sum reaches \(p\).

Exact identities; finite arithmetic windows

The variable change is exact; the finite circuit saves further work by truncating its arithmetic. Table X uses \(1.413n+2.4\sqrt n\) iterations, width \(n-i/1.413+2.3\sqrt n\) at iteration \(i\), comparison width \(40+2.3\sqrt n\), 37 special-case rounds, 65-bit corrections, and 32-bit phase comparisons. Applying these formulas requires integer rounding and clipping. In a million sampled inputs, each direction had 21 failures, counting wrong values, residual phases, and uncleared workspace. Those observations supply the statistical bound used in the success analysis.

title: VI. Optimized binary gcd iteration

body:
Subtract a square without destroying its input

After finding the slope, point addition must subtract its square from the other coordinate register. We want to change the target while keeping the slope available for the next operation. For secp256k1, both registers contain 256-bit residues modulo \(p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977\).

The required map is \(|x,y\rangle\mapsto|x,y-x^2\bmod p\rangle\). Keeping \(x\) makes it possible to reverse the update. We will first exploit the repeated terms in a square, then make their additions cheaper, and finally split the calculation into smaller squares. The integer squares are exact; modular accumulation is where the circuit uses approximations.

Use the triangle of distinct bit products

Multiplying a number by itself repeats every off-diagonal bit product. The product of bit \(i\) with bit \(j\) appears again with the indices exchanged, while a diagonal bit satisfies \(x_i^2=x_i\). We can combine the repeated terms: \[x^2=\sum_i2^{2i}x_i+\sum_{i<j}2^{i+j+1}x_ix_j.\] The diagram keeps one triangle of products. To process its rows, let \(h_i=\lfloor x/2^{i+1}\rfloor\) denote the bits above \(x_i\).

Make every step add or subtract

An ordinary row adds something only when \(x_i=1\). We instead let the bit choose a positive or negative contribution, then correct the total. The extra contributions sum to \[\sum_i2^{2i+1}h_i=\sum_jx_j(2^{2j}-2^j),\] Substituting this into the square gives \[\boxed{x^2=-x+\sum_i(2x_i-1)2^{2i+1}(h_i+x_i).}\] Thus we start from \(-x\) and apply a signed update at offset \(2i+1\) for each bit. The control selects a sign, allowing the ordinary carry circuit to run in both branches.

ControlSource presented to subtractorTarget change modulo \(2^w\)
\(x_i=0\)\(h_i\)\(-h_i\)
\(x_i=1\)\(2^w-1-h_i\)\(h_i+1\)

Let the active window shrink

As we move to higher input bits, fewer target bits remain to be updated. The active widths are \(n+1,n,\ldots,2\). The first \(n-1\) steps extend the sign with a CNOT, and the last update is itself a CNOT. Counting \(w-1\) Toffoli-type operations for a width-\(w\) adder gives \[T(n)=n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(n-i)=\frac{n(n+3)}2-1.\] This is the cost of computing one exact integer square. Accumulating it modulo the field and clearing its scratch come next.

In two's-complement notation, \(1101_2\) represents −3. Exposing another high bit must produce \(11101_2\), still −3. Extending with zero instead would produce 13 and change the signed accumulation.

Exploit the shape of the modulus

At 256 bits, we can reduce that work further by splitting the input in half. Write \(x=x_L+Bx_H\), where \(B=2^{n/2}\). Three smaller squares recover the cross term because \(2x_Lx_H=(x_L+x_H)^2-x_L^2-x_H^2\). The modulus also gives \(B^2\equiv c\), so the square subtraction becomes \[-x^2\equiv(B-1)x_L^2+(B-c)x_H^2-B(x_L+x_H)^2\pmod p.\] The sum of the halves needs one extra bit, explaining the larger third square.

Compute the low-half square into scratch, add its indicated multiple to the target, and reverse the square computation. The scratch is now free for the high-half square and then the sum-square. At 256 bits their widths are 128, 128, and 129. Computing and reversing the three leaves costs \(2[2T(128)+T(129)]=50{,}558\) Toffoli-type operations, before the other additions.

The remaining task is to add the shifted multiples modulo the prime. Here \(c=2^{32}+2^{10}-2^6+2^4+1\), so multiplication by \(c\) uses five signed shifts. Bits that cross the top of the register require an explicit correction. The appendix lesson follows those updates and explains how short carries and truncated phase comparisons enter their failure bound.

title: VII. Modular squaring

body:
The appendix supplies the arithmetic contracts

The square-subtraction circuit is built from a small operation: add a selected slice of one register into another at a chosen bit position. Understanding that operation explains both the implementation and its errors. The field is \(p=2^n-c\), with \(n=256\) and \(c=2^{32}+977\) for secp256k1.

AlgorithmsContract
4–6Randomize tables; loop over scalar windows; add one selected point.
7Preserve \(x,q\); update \(y\mapsto y-qx^2\pmod p\).
8: AddSlicePreserve source and control; add a signed shifted slice.
9: PhaseGEPreserve comparison inputs; apply the predicate as a sign.
10–11Accumulate structured multiples \(Bs\) and \(cs\).

First place this arithmetic in the algorithm. The classical tables shift every scalar branch by the same group element and exclude the point at infinity. With 16-bit windows, the first window is a direct lookup and three final windows move to classical recovery. The remaining 28 point additions follow the two-register calculation.

A short update can miss a long carry

Take \(w\) source bits beginning at position \(o\), and call their value \(a=s_{[o,o+w)}\). Shift them to target position \(t\), choose sign \(\sigma\), and optionally apply the update under control \(q\): \[v'\equiv v+q\sigma2^ta\pmod p.\] For an update below the top boundary, the circuit touches only \(w+\rho\) bits. The extra \(\rho\) bits absorb carries. A carry that travels farther is exactly the event the approximation misses.

A four-bit local update \(0010+0011=0101\) fits its window. The update \(1111+0011=1\,0010\) needs a fifth bit; leaving that bit untouched loses the carry.

Fold overflow back into low bits

When the update reaches the top of the register, we cannot simply discard overflow. An overflow bit \(h\) represents \(h2^n\), and the field identity \(2^n\equiv c\) tells us to add \(hc\) back at the bottom. The two expressions below show the integer sum and its modular replacement.

Before folding

Before reduction, the low register contains \(z\) and the overflow records \(v+a=z+h2^n\).

After folding

After reduction, the same residue is represented by \(z+hc\pmod p\).

That correction uses only the lowest \(\kappa\) bits, so a carry escaping this second window is another failure event. To subtract, the circuit surrounds addition with \(F(v)=p-1-v\). Adding \(c\) and complementing implements this map on valid branches, and \(F(F(v)+a)=v-a\pmod p\) gives the desired subtraction.

A correct integer can still have the wrong sign

Once overflow has been used, its qubit must be cleared. An X measurement with result \(m\) transfers the sign \((-1)^{mh}\) to the retained registers. On the top-wrap branch with \(m=1\), the circuit applies \((-1)^q\) and a comparison phase to cancel it. PhaseGE computes \((-1)^{q[x\ge y]}\) exactly for the prefixes it receives; the approximation is supplying only \(\delta\) high bits.

For example, 101000 and 101011 differ as six-bit integers, but their first three bits agree. A comparison of those prefixes can therefore reconstruct the wrong overflow. The output integer remains correct while its amplitude has the wrong sign. This is why the error analysis must follow phases as well as values.

Shifts need their overflow correction too

The same overflow principle applies to shifted multiples. Writing \(s=s_L+Bs_H\) gives \(Bs\equiv Bs_L+cs_H\). The five signed shifts for \(c\) omit high pieces whose combined value is \[h_s=s_{[224,256)}+s_{[246,256)}-s_{[250,256)}+s_{[252,256)}.\] Algorithm 11 restores their contribution by adding \(ch_s\). Since \(0\le h_s\le c-3\), this correction fits in 65 bits and can be computed exactly, used, and uncomputed.

Assemble the bound

The complete three-square update contains 16 local additions, nine wrapping additions, and 26 complement sites. For a uniformly masked target and the helper conditions in Appendix A, a union bound over their value and phase failures gives \[p_{\rm sq}\le\left(1+\frac cp\right)\left(\frac{16}{2^\rho}+\frac{35c}{2^\kappa}+\frac9{2^\delta}+\frac{9c}{2^{256}}\right)<2^{-26.59}.\] The numerical result uses \(\rho=\delta=32\) and \(\kappa=65\). Each term now has a concrete origin: a carry window, a modular correction, or a phase comparison.

title: Appendix A. Algorithms

body:
Store the computation instead of its inverse

Point addition needs to multiply or divide a register by another register without retaining a separate answer. For a nonzero \(x\) modulo an odd prime \(p\), the map \((x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)\) is reversible: division by \(x\) undoes it. The challenge is to implement it with little temporary storage.

Schrottenloher's construction records how binary gcd reduces \((p,x)\), then uses that record to act on \(y\). The record shares storage with the shrinking remainders. This baseline uses 1462 logical qubits, including a 16-bit window, and about \(2^{25.78}\) Toffoli-type operations for secp256k1. IonQ builds on it by changing the additions and squaring, then scheduling the result on its architecture.

Each gcd step has a small reversible record

Start with integer remainders \((u,v)=(p,x)\). Record whether \(v\) is odd, \(a=v\bmod2\), and whether the odd branch requires a swap, \(m=a[u>v]\). Swap when needed, subtract \(au\) from \(v\), and halve. Repeating these reductions reaches \((1,0)\), since the prime and a nonzero residue are coprime.

Record constructionIts inverse
Swap if \(m=1\)Double the second register
Subtract \(au\)Add \(au\) back
Halve the even resultReverse the recorded swap

Every reduction can be reversed once its decisions are known. The endpoint together with the history, denoted \(\rho_x\), therefore retains the input's information. This is the representation we need: it describes how to act on another register without first producing an inverse in its own register.

Apply the history to another vector

For multiplication, begin with field registers \((r,s)=(y,0)\) and replay the reductions backward. Each reversed step doubles \(s\), adds \(ar\), and undoes the recorded swap. The resulting pair is \((0,xy)\). Forward replay gives division. The complete construction is \[|x,y\rangle\longrightarrow|\rho_x,y\rangle\longrightarrow|\rho_x,xy\rangle\longrightarrow|x,xy\rangle.\] Reversing record construction at the end restores \(x\) and releases the history. The replay proof explains why this works for every numerator.

Three decisions fit in five qubits

The record can itself be compressed. An even remainder never triggers a swap, so the possible pairs \((a,m)\) are only 00, 10, and 11. Three decisions have 27 possibilities and fit in five qubits. The circuit below uses five Toffoli gates to compress their six wires and clear the unused wire.

The history \((11)(00)(10)\) enters as 110010 and the circuit returns 011010. The last zero can be reused while the first five bits retain the history. This is a reversible encoding on the allowed inputs.

The shrinking values pay for the growing history

As the remainders shrink, their released high bits can hold those compressed decisions. The circuit includes \(2.3\sqrt n\) width padding and roughly \(1.413n+2.4\sqrt n\) iterations to accommodate the sampled distribution of reductions. The leading history size is \((5/3)(1.413n)\approx2.355n\); with the two replay registers, this gives \(4.355n+O(\sqrt n)\) qubits before additional adder workspace.

Where approximation enters

This storage saving uses finite budgets. Too many iterations, unexpectedly large remainders, missed carries, or incorrect phase comparisons can cause failure. IonQ changes some of those operations through its odd-register update and specialized squarer, so it evaluates the resulting failures again for its own circuit.

title: Reference [2]. Schrottenloher’s arithmetic construction

body:
Pay for the AND once

An adder repeatedly needs to know whether two bits are both 1. It uses that AND value to form the next carry, then no longer needs it. We can save non-Clifford gates by treating this value as temporary information and clearing it through measurement.

For bits \(a,b\), the temporary computation is \(|a,b,0\rangle\mapsto|a,b,ab\rangle\). Gidney prepares this value using four T resources. After it has been used, measurement and a Clifford correction erase it without further T resources. The target begins at zero, and the controls remain available for that correction; these are the conditions that enable the saving.

The four-T computation

The circuit below shows where the four resources enter. One is the input state \(|T\rangle=T|+\rangle\); the others are one T and two \(T^\dagger\) gates. Here \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\) and \(S=T^2\). All remaining operations in this redraw of Gidney's Figure 3 are Clifford gates.

Erase information without erasing coherence

To clear the AND, measure its ancilla in the X basis. For outcome \(m\), the remaining state becomes \[\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}|a,b,ab\rangle\longrightarrow\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}(-1)^{mab}|a,b\rangle.\] The sign appears only when both controls are 1. Applying \(\mathrm{CZ}\) when \(m=1\) therefore removes it exactly, for any input amplitudes.

Control branchPhase when \(m=1\)CZ correctionNet phase
\(00,01,10\)\(+1\)\(+1\)\(+1\)
\(11\)\(-1\)\(-1\)\(+1\)

For input \(|++\rangle\), omitting this correction would leave the computational-basis probabilities unchanged. It would nevertheless place a minus sign on the \(|11\rangle\) component for one measurement outcome and entangle the controls. The phase correction is what makes the erasure a valid quantum operation.

One nonlinear computation per carry

Now apply the construction to a carry. At bit position \(i\), XOR gives the sum \(s_i=a_i\oplus b_i\oplus c_i\), where \(c_i\) is the incoming carry. The outgoing carry can be written as \[c_{i+1}=c_i\oplus[(a_i\oplus c_i)(b_i\oplus c_i)].\] Only the product in brackets is nonlinear. It requires one temporary AND; the surrounding operations are XORs.

No incoming carry

When the incoming carry is 0, the formula reduces to \(c_{i+1}=a_ib_i\). A new carry appears only if both input bits are 1.

Incoming carry

When the incoming carry is 1, it becomes \(c_{i+1}=1\oplus(1-a_i)(1-b_i)\). The incoming 1 already supplies half of the required total, so either input bit can produce the next carry.

The cost moves into workspace and measurements

With zero incoming carry and no retained carry-out, an \(n\)-bit adder needs \(n-1\) temporary ANDs. It therefore uses \(4n-4\) T resources and \(n-1\) measurement erasures. IonQ records these as \(n-1\) Toffoli-type computations. Their ancillas remain occupied until erased, linking the gate saving to the available workspace.

The erasures still require measurements, feedforward, and access to the controls. Their scheduling contributes to the runtime even though they consume no additional T resources. The same carry construction also supports add-or-subtract: conditional complements select the sign while leaving the nonlinear carry work unchanged.

body:
The task: divide without storing an inverse

Suppose the numerator is 4 and the denominator is 5 modulo 13. Division should return 6, since \(5\cdot6\equiv4\). We want a circuit that performs this replacement even when its inputs are in superposition. For a known odd prime \(p\) and nonzero denominator \(x\), the operation is \[|x\rangle|y\rangle\longmapsto|x\rangle|yx^{-1}\bmod p\rangle.\]

In point addition, \(x\) and \(y\) are coordinate differences and the quotient is the slope. A direct approach would compute \(x^{-1}\), multiply it by \(y\), then clear the inverse. The recorded-gcd construction instead applies the inverse through the sequence that reduces \((p,x)\) to \((1,0)\).

The central observation is that, once their branch decisions are fixed, those reductions are linear operations on a pair of field values. Applying the same sequence to a pair containing \(y\) gives the quotient. We therefore need to retain the decisions, rather than an explicit inverse.

What the record contains

Begin with integer remainders \((u,v)=(p,x)\). Keep \(u\) odd and repeat the following steps while \(v\) is nonzero. Each step records whether to swap and whether to subtract before halving.

  1. When v is odd and smaller than u, record \(m_i=1\) and exchange the remainders; otherwise record 0.
  2. After that exchange, record the parity \(a_i=v\bmod2\) of the second remainder.
  3. Subtract \(a_iu\) from v and halve the even result: \(v\leftarrow(v-a_iu)/2\).

The endpoint is \((1,0)\). The ordered decisions \((m_i,a_i)\) form the record \(R(x)\), together with indicators for active steps. In superposition, branches finish at different times, so the circuit uses a fixed schedule and applies identities to finished branches. The record remains quantum information correlated with \(x\).

Keep the current numbers; save only the decisions

To build the record, we still need the current gcd remainders. Start with (13,5): inspect them, decide to swap and subtract, then halve to reach (5,4). Save the decisions and inspect this new pair to choose the next step. The distinction is what we keep from earlier steps: a short decision record or a separate register for every numerical pair.

Build the record while updating one pair

Each step below updates the current pair and appends two bits to the record. The first bit says whether to swap; the second says whether to subtract. Every active step then halves the second remainder. The vertical lines connect each update to the decisions it saves; they do not denote measurements.

The decision bits make the update reversible. To undo the first step, start from (5,4), double the second entry to get (5,8), add the first to get (5,13), then undo the swap to recover (13,5). No saved copy of (13,5) is needed.

Alternatively, keep every intermediate pair

For comparison, give each next pair a fresh register initialized to zero. A reversible block computes the next pair into that register while preserving the previous pair. The dots indicate which existing pair supplies the input to each block.

After three steps, the first construction holds (5,1) plus six decision bits; the second holds four numerical pairs. This comparison shows what recording decisions replaces. It does not claim that every alternative gcd circuit stores a full history. The actual space saving also depends on packing the shrinking remainders and keeping the arithmetic workspace clean.

Once the record is built, replay it once on the numerator to obtain the slope. Then reverse record construction to restore the denominator and clear the history. Reusing the record many times is not the reason for this construction.

Three blocks, with explicit contracts

We can now separate the construction into three operations. Start with record register \(R=0\) and field registers \((s,t)=(0,y)\). Build \(R(x)\), use it to transform \((s,t)\), then erase it using the unchanged denominator. The table gives the register contract for each box in the circuit.

BoxAction
Make record\(|x,0\rangle\mapsto|x,R(x)\rangle\): reversibly compute the denominator’s gcd decisions, preserving x.
Apply recordUse the stored decisions as controls on s,t. Starting from (0,y), the result is \((yx^{-1},0)\). The next drawing expands one step.
Erase recordReverse Make record: \(|x,R(x)\rangle\mapsto|x,0\rangle\). It does not act on the quotient.

Open “Apply record”

During replay, read each stored pair \((m_i,a_i)\) and apply its swap, subtraction, and halving to \((s,t)\). The decisions must come from the denominator's record. Recomputing them from the numerator pair would produce a different sequence and lose the division identity.

The replay takes place in the field, so halving an odd value must still be reversible. For example, half of 9 modulo 13 is 11, because \(2\cdot11\equiv9\). For any canonical value \(t\), use

\[h_p(t)=\begin{cases}t/2,&t\text{ even},\\(t+p)/2,&t\text{ odd},\end{cases}\qquad h_p(t)=2^{-1}t\pmod p.\]

The extra prime makes an odd numerator even before integer division by two. Doubling modulo \(p\) reverses the result, so no information is discarded. Both the subtraction and halving subcircuits return their own temporary qubits to zero.

Why these steps produce the quotient

To prove the result, fix \(x\), hence fix its record. Each step is a swap, a shear from subtraction, and multiplication by \(2^{-1}\) on the second entry. Their matrices are \[M_i=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-a_i&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}^{m_i}.\] Let \(M_x=M_L\cdots M_1\) denote their product over the \(L\) active steps.

We already know what this product does to the original remainders: it takes \((p,x)\) to \((1,0)\). Modulo \(p\), that statement becomes

\[M_x\binom0x=\binom10.\]

The numerator pair \((0,y)\) is \(yx^{-1}\) times \((0,x)\). Applying a linear map preserves that scalar relation, giving

\[M_x\binom0y=yx^{-1}M_x\binom0x=\binom{yx^{-1}}0.\]

Thus forward replay places \(yx^{-1}\) in the first register and clears the second. A SWAP puts the quotient back where the numerator began. Reversing replay instead maps \((y,0)\) to \((0,xy)\), implementing multiplication. The matrices establish the identity; the circuit executes the recorded elementary operations.

One record, followed all the way through

Return to \(p=13,x=5,y=4\). The left side of the table builds the record from integer remainders. The right side applies each same decision modulo 13 to \((0,4)\). Comparing the two columns shows how one reduction sequence serves two different inputs.

Step(mᵢ,aᵢ)Remainders (u,v)Replay (s,t)
Start—(13,5)(0,4)
1(1,1)(5,4)(4,11)
2(0,0)(5,2)(4,12)
3(0,0)(5,1)(4,6)
4(1,1)(1,2)(6,12)
5(0,0)(1,1)(6,6)
6(0,1)(1,0)(6,0)

In the first replay step, swap to \((4,0)\), subtract to \((4,9)\), and halve 9 to obtain \((4,11)\). Continue with the recorded decisions until the pair becomes \((6,0)\). Checking \(5\cdot6\equiv4\pmod{13}\) confirms the quotient.

Why the quantum record must be cleared

The record still contains information about \(x\) after replay. Measuring it directly could reveal the denominator and disturb its superposition. Instead, reverse record construction using the preserved \(x\). This clears the record without acting on the quotient. Any internal measurement erasure must include its phase correction.

What makes this a space-saving representation

The separate wires in the diagram make the logic easy to follow. The compact Dialog implementation shares storage: as the remainders shrink, their cleared high bits hold the growing history. Reversing this representation change after replay restores the denominator and frees the same storage.

Reference [52] develops Dialog for polynomial arithmetic; Schrottenloher applies the idea to integer binary gcd. IonQ then changes the stored variables to lower the cost of each addition. The replay derivation above uses exact ordinary-variable steps. The finite widths and truncated arithmetic in the resource estimate are assessed in its failure analysis.

With the replay understood, the odd-register construction explains the cheaper iteration. Returning to point addition, the quotient is exactly the slope needed for the next coordinate update.

body:
Put the control on complements instead of carries

Consider a control bit that chooses between adding and subtracting a number. We can make that choice without controlling every carry. For an \(n\)-bit target, complementing all bits before and after an ordinary addition changes its sign. The source and control remain unchanged.

For example, in four bits, complement 6 to obtain 9, add 3 to obtain 12, then complement to obtain 3: the net effect is subtracting 3 from 6. In general, with \(A_u(z)=z+u\pmod{2^n}\) and \(J(z)=2^n-1-z\), \[J A_u J(z)=z-u\pmod{2^n}.\] A control bit switches the two complements on or off through CNOTs. The nonlinear carry circuit remains an ordinary adder.

The control choice changes the non-Clifford count

Once the sign control is carried by complements, the nonlinear work is the same as an ordinary adder. Compare that with a control that must disable the addition entirely.

Operation in this adder familyNo carry-outCarry-out retained
Add\(n-1\)\(n\)
Add or subtract\(n-1\)\(n\)
Add or skip\(2n-1\)\(2n+1\)

The table counts Toffoli-type computations for this adder family, with and without an extra overflow bit. Choosing a sign has the same nonlinear cost as addition; choosing whether to add costs more. The added CNOTs still require physical access and schedule time.

Recover an ordinary product from signed additions

To use this saving in multiplication, every digit must select a sign. Writing \(x=\sum_i2^ix_i\), the signed contributions satisfy \[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(2x_i-1)2^iy=2xy-(2^n-1)y.\] Their sum is not yet the product, but its correction is simple: add \((2^n-1)y\), then halve. Each digit now uses the cheaper add-or-subtract operation.

A zero input bit now contributes \(-2^iy\), while a one contributes \(+2^iy\). Summing the known correction restores the contributions removed by changing the zero branches.

Unsigned carry-out introduces a second correction

Retaining carry-out changes the integer represented by a subtraction branch. It returns \(z+2^n-y\), so digit \(i\) contributes \[(1-x_i)2^{n+i}+(2x_i-1)2^iy.\] Summing yields \(R=2xy+2^{2n}-2^n(x+1+y)+y\). The circuit below removes these offsets, leaving \(2xy\). Its final low bit is zero, allowing division by two through wire relabeling.

The resulting multiplier, and what IonQ imports

Including those corrections, the full integer multiplier costs \(n^2+4n+3\), compared with \(2n^2+n\) for the reference controlled-adder construction. If only the product modulo \(2^n\) is needed, high contributions can be dropped, giving \(n^2/2+3n/2\) instead of \(n^2\). These counts include the conventions of the particular circuits being compared.

IonQ uses the signed non-modular arithmetic as a building block. It specializes equal operands into a square and supplies its own reduction for the secp256k1 prime. Litinski's full windowed Montgomery construction is therefore separate from the implementation analyzed here.

In a square, equal off-diagonal products can also be combined: \[x^2=\sum_i2^{2i}x_i+\sum_{i<j}2^{i+j+1}x_ix_j.\] Together with signed additions, this gives \(n(n+3)/2-1\) Toffoli-type operations. The gcd circuit reaches signed addition through the different identity \(\widetilde v=v+(1-a)u\). In both cases the algebra first changes the computation so that choosing a sign preserves its intended result.

body:
Recover two cross terms from one product

Multiplying two split numbers ordinarily needs four smaller products. Karatsuba recovers the two cross terms from one product of sums, reducing that number to three. We first work over integers; afterward the special field modulus will simplify how the pieces are accumulated.

Write \(x=x_L+Bx_H\) and \(y=y_L+By_H\), with halves below \(B=2^{n/2}\). Compute \[z_0=x_Ly_L,\quad z_2=x_Hy_H,\quad z_1=(x_L+x_H)(y_L+y_H).\] Expanding the product of sums shows that subtracting \(z_0\) and \(z_2\) leaves both cross terms. Restoring their place values gives \[\boxed{xy=z_0+B(z_1-z_0-z_2)+B^2z_2.}\]

Direct expansion

Ordinary multiplication computes each diagonal and each cross term separately, for four half-size products.

Karatsuba expansion

Karatsuba keeps the two diagonals and obtains both cross terms from one product of sums, followed by additions and subtractions.

One split can be better than full recursion

Repeating the split gives \(M(n)=3M(n/2)+O(n)\), with exponent \(\log_2 3\approx1.585\). A quantum implementation also pays for temporary registers and their cleanup at every level. The paper chooses one split and uses exact schoolbook squarers on the resulting 128- and 129-bit inputs.

The product of sums becomes a square

For squaring, set the two inputs equal. The product-of-sums term becomes another square: \[x^2=x_L^2+B[(x_L+x_H)^2-x_L^2-x_H^2]+B^2x_H^2.\] Each half is at most \(B-1\), so their sum can reach \(2B-2\). That extra bit is the reason the third leaf has width 129 rather than 128.

Fold the high square through the modulus

Point addition needs to subtract the square modulo \(p=2^n-c\). Since \(B^2=2^n\equiv c\), replacing the high place value and collecting terms gives \[-x^2\equiv(B-1)x_L^2+(B-c)x_H^2-B(x_L+x_H)^2\pmod p.\] We now have three smaller squares with coefficients implemented by shifts and short multiples.

Reuse scratch only after reversing the square

Compute one square into scratch, add its multiple to the target, then reverse the square computation. The scratch is correlated with the input until that reversal; measuring it in the computational basis would reveal input information. Clearing it coherently makes the same register available for the next square.

StageSource half-registerSquare scratch
Prepare the sum\(x_H\to x_H+x_L\)\(0\)
Compute; update target\(x_H+x_L\)\((x_H+x_L)^2\)
Reverse square; subtract \(x_L\)\(x_H\)\(0\)

The sum-square needs one additional cleanup step: after reversing the square, subtract \(x_L\) from the enlarged high-half register. This restores \(x_H\) and clears its extra bit. The two individual-half squares use the same scratch sequence without forming that sum.

Count the leaves separately from their accumulation

The exact leaf formula \(T(m)=m(m+3)/2-1\) gives costs 8383, 8383, and 8513. Computing and reversing all three totals \(50{,}558\) Toffoli-type operations. Forming the half-sum, accumulating shifted multiples, modular corrections, and scheduling are additional costs.

The split identity and leaf squares remain exact throughout. Approximation enters when the modular target updates truncate carry propagation or phase comparisons. This separation lets the failure analysis identify the approximate helper operations while retaining an exact derivation of the square being computed.
